chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Fudayl from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who killed a pigeon from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Haram) while he was not in a state of Ihram. He said: 'Upon him is its value, which is one dirham; he gives it in charity or buys food for the pigeons of the Sanctuary. And if he killed it while he was in Ihram within the Sanctuary, then upon him is a sheep and the value of the pigeon.'
And it also indicates that whenever it was permissible (non-Ihram) and he slaughtered it in the Sanctuary, it does not necessitate upon him more than the value.

key_terms.اَلْحَرَمِ: The Sanctuary (specifically Mecca/Medina), a sacred area with specific rules
key_terms.دِرْهَمٌ: A dirham (silver coin), specified here as the value
key_terms.شَاةٌ: A sheep (used as a specific fine/penalty)
key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: One in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the penalty for killing a pigeon in the Haram for someone in Ihram versus someone not in Ihram?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), highlighting the distinct legal status of the Haram's wildlife as a protected entity where killing incurs a specific financial penalty (qimah) rather than a general blood price. The hadith clarifies that while Ihram intensifies the penalty by adding a sacrificial animal (sheep), the base compensation for the bird remains consistent, underscoring the sanctity of the sanctuary's ecosystem in Shia jurisprudence. This serves as a foundational text for understanding the ecological ethics and ritual purity laws governing pilgrims within the holy precincts.
